newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-LINDH TAKES SPOTLIGHT AND STREET'S TITLE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-LINDH TAKES SPOTLIGHT AND STREET'S TITLE.

text.p: American Hilary Lindh emerged from two years in the shadow of Picabo Street to take her absent compatriot's world championship downhill title on Saturday.
Last year in Sierra Nevada, Lindh had to settle for bronze and watch the more flamboyant and outspoken Street enjoy the glory of an Alpine skiing gold medal.
Lindh seriously considered retirement after that.
But the 27-year-old Lindh found that American hopes rested on her shoulders after Street tore her cruciate knee ligament in a downhill in December and was forced to write off the rest of the season.
In Sestriere, the unfancied Lindh, who has not stood on a World Cup podium for two years, stunned everyone by posting the fasting time down the Kandahar-Banchetta piste.
When asked how it felt to have conquered Street's title, Lindh said: "I think it's a special feeling no matter who won last year.
"I'm sorry Picabo is not here, she would have loved this course. I'm looking forward to seeing her and sharing this victory with her.
"We are not close friends but are on friendly terms and wish the best for each other," said Lindh, denying rumours that the tough rivalry between the pair had made them enemies.
Lindh had been the number one on the small United States ski team after claiming 1992 Olympic downhill silver and recording three World Cup wins in 1994 at Sierra Nevada, Vail and Lake Louise.
But when Street won the same Olympic medal in 1994 -- a race in which Lindh finished a disappointing seventh -- Lindh suddenly found she was playing second fiddle.
Street went on to upstage Lindh the following season by winning six World Cup downhills and becoming the first American to lift the trophy in the discipline.

With the exception of last year's world championship bronze, Lindh's recent showing has been anything but impressive. She last stood on a World Cup rostrum in 1994 when she won the second of two back-to-back downhills in Lake Louise.
She has also been fighting back troubles and has to take medicine regularly.
"I have to be careful with my back and have to make sure I warm up in the mornings," said Lindh, who also suffered two serious knee injuries in 1987 and 1993.
Last year she came close to quitting the sport.
"There are other things I want to do outside of ski racing and it's getting difficult to put these things back," said Lindh, a biology student in her native Juneau, Alaska.
"Even at the start of the season, I didn't know if I had made the right decision. But I'm very proud that I stuck it out and hung in there."

North Americans are legendary for faring better at big events than on the World Cup. Tommy Moe, for example, became Olympic downhill champion in 1994 although he had never won a World Cup race before that.
"When you spend so many months so far away from home, it's difficult to keep the continuous good level required in the World Cup," said Lindh.
"For us in the United States, the only thing that matters are the big events. It's the only way you get recognition so that automatically makes it our big goal.
"We have no pressure to do well. Unlike the Europeans, we don't get mobbed for autographs or by journalists. We can concentrate only on our skiing," she added.
Whether Saturday's gold medal will be enough to keep Lindh in ski racing until next year's Nagano Olympics is still uncertain.
"As far as next year is concerned it's all up in the air at this point. I'm not sure," she said.
